title: SMRs: a short history of a nuclear pipe dream
gist: Historian Paul Josephson argues small modular reactors are a 70-year 'pipe dream': only two operate worldwide, there is still no serial factory production, every generation from Cold War military units to NuScale has overrun budgets, and nuclear LCOE (~$110/MWh) is far above solar and wind. He concludes AI data-centre demand, military subsidies and government backing do not make SMRs a good bet for investors, though military programmes (Pele, Janus) will push ahead regardless.

themes.theme: SMR economics and the cost-overrun record

insights.claim: Only two SMRs are operating anywhere in the world, one of which (a Russian floating plant) took 13 years to bring online, despite over 70 SMR projects worth roughly $16 billion in development.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Commercial SMR timelines priced by markets are not supported by any deployment track record.
insights.quote: only two SMRs are operating anywhere, one of which, a floating plant in Russia, took 13 years to bring online

insights.claim: Nuclear LCOE was estimated at $110/MWh in 2023 and is forecast to stay flat to 2050, versus solar at $55/MWh falling to $25/MWh and onshore wind at $40/MWh falling to $35/MWh.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: The widening cost gap undermines nuclear's competitiveness unless firmness is heavily priced.
insights.quote: its LCOE (levelised cost of electricity) estimated at $110/MWh in 2023 and forecast to remain the same up to 2050

insights.claim: A study of 180 nuclear power plants found 175 exceeded their initial budgets by an average of 117% and took 64% longer than projected.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Base rates for nuclear capex overruns should anchor any valuation of nuclear developers.
insights.quote: 175 of them exceeded the initial budget by an average of 117 per cent and took 64 per cent longer than projected

insights.claim: Georgia's Vogtle plant came in seven years late and $17 billion over budget, with ratepayers paying billions before receiving any electricity, which is why the industry pivoted its hopes to SMRs.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Ratepayer and regulated-utility exposure to nuclear overruns is a recurring risk.
insights.quote: seven years late, $17 billion over budget
insights.locator: The nuclear industry has nevertheless pinned

insights.claim: NuScale, the only NRC-certified SMR design, was cancelled in 2023 after forecast power costs rose 53% from $58/MWh to $89/MWh and project costs rose from $5.3 to $9.3 billion before construction, even with $4 billion in federal tax subsidies and a $30/MWh IRA break.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Even the most advanced, subsidised SMR failed on cost: a key precedent for current SMR equities.
insights.quote: forecast costs rose 53 per cent from $58/MWh to $89/MWh, and overall from $5.3 to $9.3 billion, even before construction began

insights.claim: SMRs lose the claimed size advantage because developers cluster multiple units for competitiveness (NuScale planned 6-12, Ontario's Darlington four), so plants remain large, need exclusion zones and round-the-clock security.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: 'Small' does not translate into lower siting or security costs.

insights.claim: China's 125 MWe ACP100 Linglong One, costing an estimated 5 billion yuan, has a higher per-megawatt cost than large-scale nuclear plants, and its first HTR-PM SMR cost $3 billion and took ten years.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Diseconomies of small scale are visible even in the most aggressive nuclear builder.
insights.quote: it has a higher per-megawatt cost than large-scale NPPs

insights.claim: SMRs will only be cost-competitive with wind and solar when produced in large numbers of standardised models, which the author calls a pipe dream.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: The investment case hinges on a serial-production condition that has never been met.
insights.quote: SMRs will only be competitive in cost with wind, solar and other forms of energy when they are produced in sufficient numbers of standard models

insights.claim: The author concludes that 70 years of high costs, one-off designs and technical underperformance make SMRs a bad bet for investors.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Direct bearish call on the SMR investment theme.
insights.quote: 70 years of high costs, one-off designs and technical underperformance indicate that they are a bad bet for investors
insights.locator: SMRs heighten the risk of terrorist

insights.claim: No factory exists that produces SMR reactor vessels and components serially; the claim of 'off-the-shelf' modules is unsupported.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Supply-chain bottlenecks for heavy nuclear components are a hidden constraint on any SMR rollout.
insights.quote: there is still no factory that produces the components serially

insights.claim: The Soviet Atommash factory in Volgodonsk, meant to produce eight reactor pressure vessels a year, had built only 14 in total by 2017, mostly in the 2000s after Putin-era subsidies revived it.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: The only historical attempt at factory-built reactors badly underdelivered.
insights.quote: Although Atommash was intended to produce eight pressure vessels annually, by 2017 only 14 in all had been manufactured
insights.locator: The one attempt at factory production

insights.claim: Molten salt reactors require costly specialised alloys, become extremely radioactive in pumps and heat exchangers, need robot-only maintenance, and lack any manufacturing industry for suitable parts.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Advanced-design start-ups face unsolved materials problems that may extend timelines indefinitely.
insights.quote: there is no manufacturing industry for the right high-temperature and radiation-resistant parts
insights.locator: In general, molten salt designs face

insights.claim: Fifty years after the Molten Salt Reactor Experiment, no material is known to perform satisfactorily in the high-radiation, high-temperature corrosive environment of a molten salt reactor.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Materials risk is a core technical risk for Gen IV nuclear ventures.
insights.quote: Even today, no material can perform satisfactorily in the high-radiation, high-temperature, and corrosive environment inside a molten salt reactor
insights.locator: Molten salt reactors have a poor record

insights.claim: Former nuclear executive Arnie Gundersen notes every steam generator built for US reactors has failed prematurely, and SMRs will use the same technology.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Component reliability issues carry over into SMR operating economics.
insights.quote: every steam generator ever built for US reactors has failed prematurely

themes.theme: AI data-centre demand as the new SMR narrative

insights.claim: A major driver of the SMR revival is AI data-centre electricity demand, but round-the-clock power needs do not by themselves justify nuclear, still less small reactors.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: AI-power trades in SMR names rest on a narrative the author views as unfounded.
insights.quote: Data centres require round-the-clock power, but that does not in itself make the case for nuclear, still less for small reactors.

insights.claim: In January 2026 Meta announced plans with Vistra, TerraPower and Oklo to boost advanced nuclear development, while the Bezos Earth Fund committed to helping build a buyer orderbook for standardised large US reactors.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Big-tech offtake commitments are the key demand catalyst underpinning nuclear developer valuations.
insights.locator: A major reason for the rebirth

insights.claim: Peter Thiel's Founders Fund-backed uranium enrichment start-up General Matter won a $900 million Department of Energy contract in January 2026.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Federal money is flowing into domestic enrichment, a fuel-cycle chokepoint.
insights.locator: A major reason for the rebirth

insights.claim: TerraPower's 345 MW Natrium sodium fast reactor in Wyoming, backed by Bill Gates and up to $2 billion from the DOE, received an NRC construction permit in March 2026 and is building supply chains with South Korean firms.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Natrium is the bellwether advanced-reactor project for the AI-power thesis.
insights.locator: The efforts to power AI with SMRs

insights.claim: Big-tech billionaires are pushing for accelerated SMR licensing and have the ear of a nuclear-friendly White House, while promoters seek relaxed rules such as smaller emergency planning zones to cut costs rather than because SMRs are proven safer.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Regulatory loosening is a policy catalyst for nuclear developers but carries safety and backlash tail risk.
insights.quote: Big tech billionaires are pushing for accelerated licensing – and they have the ear of a friendly fan of nuclear power in the White House.

themes.theme: Military SMRs as the real driver

insights.claim: Any real SMR progress will come, as in the Cold War, from militaries, which governments are determinedly subsidising.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Defence budgets, not commercial economics, are the more reliable revenue source for microreactor contractors.
insights.quote: Any real progress in bringing SMRs online will come, as it did during the Cold War, from the military.
insights.locator: Any real progress in bringing SMRs

insights.claim: The Army's Janus Program awarded up to $2.2 billion to Antares Nuclear, BWXT, General Atomics, Radiant Industries and Westinghouse for microreactors at five bases, with over 20 envisaged and the first due by 2028.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Named contractors stand to benefit from defence-funded microreactor orders.

insights.claim: The Pentagon's Project Pele truck-mounted microreactor, built by BWXT, is three years behind schedule but will proceed because of a White House executive order on advanced nuclear for national security.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Policy mandates insulate defence nuclear projects from delays that would kill commercial ones.
insights.quote: Already three years behind schedule
insights.locator: INL is the site of the 1961

insights.claim: Historically over 700 SMRs found their main application in US and Soviet nuclear submarines, and only the state could absorb their costs.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: SMR success has historically required a cost-insensitive state buyer.
insights.quote: Only the state could absorb the enormous costs of these projects.
insights.locator: None of this is especially new

insights.claim: Rolls-Royce claimed in 2021 its SMR consortium would create 40,000 jobs, add £100 billion to the economy and open a £400 billion export market, yet the first SMR at Wylfa is not close to construction.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Treat UK SMR economic-impact claims with heavy skepticism.
insights.locator: The major nuclear nations have hopped

insights.claim: Russia's first floating nuclear plant, the 70 MW Akademik Lomonosov, was three times over budget and years late, and Russian industry is 35 vessels behind its target for Northern Sea Route icebreakers and floating plants.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Russian Arctic nuclear ambitions, and the NSR shipping timeline, are slipping.
insights.quote: Russian industry is 35 vessels behind target.
insights.locator: Russia’s indefatigable Rosatom is most proud

insights.claim: China's nuclear industry has overtaken the US as the most active, pledging 150 new reactors over 15 years and 200 GW by 2035, almost four times current capacity, a target the author deems impossible but indicative of full commitment.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: China will dominate nuclear build-out volume even if it misses headline targets.
insights.quote: The impossible-to-reach target nevertheless indicates full commitment.

insights.claim: In March 2026 the European Commission endorsed SMRs, projecting 17-53 GW of EU SMR capacity by 2050 and €241 billion of total nuclear investment needed, despite none being under construction.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: EU policy support may channel public money into SMRs irrespective of economics.
insights.locator: In March 2026, against this uncertain record

insights.claim: EDF already redesigned its Nuward SMR in 2024, abandoning the twin-reactor 340 MWe concept for a 400 MWe version, with a first unit in France targeted for the 2030s; France 2030 allocates about €300 million to modular reactors.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Even incumbents are struggling to settle SMR designs, pushing deployment into the 2030s.

insights.claim: Canada's first SMR project uses four GE Vernova Hitachi BWRX-300 units at Darlington, with CNL also pushing SMRs to replace diesel at remote Arctic mining sites.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: BWRX-300 at Darlington is the key Western test case for SMR cost delivery.

insights.claim: Germany's nuclear safety agency says current knowledge does not support the claim that SMR concepts achieve a higher safety level in principle.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Regulatory relief premised on inherent safety could be contested.
insights.quote: based on the current state of knowledge it is not possible to state that a higher safety level is achieved by SMR concepts in principle

insights.claim: A US National Academies committee found SMRs would have high capital costs and technology gaps, be neither portable nor powerful enough for Army needs, enable proliferation and offer terrorist 'dirty bomb' targets.
insights.speaker: Paul Josephson
insights.so_what: Security and proliferation concerns are an underpriced regulatory and political risk for distributed reactors.
insights.locator: SMRs heighten the risk of terrorist
